predictions.explanation:
The prediction’s time horizon is five years from the recording date of **29 March 2025**, i.e., through about **March 2030**. As of **30 November 2025**, we are only ~8 months into that window, so it is too early to know whether China will *ultimately* fail to produce a GPU/accelerator platform competitive with Nvidia’s leading edge.

Current evidence suggests **China is still behind Nvidia at the top end**, though it is catching up:

- Huawei’s **Ascend 910B/920C** class chips are generally described as reaching roughly **60–80% of Nvidia H100-class performance** depending on metric and configuration, still short of Nvidia’s latest Hopper/Blackwell accelerators. ([c.poorc.com](https://c.poorc.com/t/chinas-domestic-gpu-industry-the-road-to-catching-up-amid-explosive-growth/780?utm_source=openai))
- Analyses of Chinese AI chips (Huawei, Cambricon, Biren, MetaX, etc.) consistently note performance and efficiency gaps versus Nvidia’s most advanced data-center GPUs, due in part to older process nodes (7 nm vs Nvidia’s 4 nm), weaker HBM, and a much less mature software ecosystem compared with CUDA. ([c.poorc.com](https://c.poorc.com/t/chinas-domestic-gpu-industry-the-road-to-catching-up-amid-explosive-growth/780?utm_source=openai))
- Even optimistic Chinese and foreign observers usually frame domestic GPUs as **approaching mid‑ to high‑range Nvidia products from earlier generations (e.g., A100 / H20)**, with roadmaps projecting potential parity only late in the decade. ([c.poorc.com](https://c.poorc.com/t/chinas-domestic-gpu-industry-the-road-to-catching-up-amid-explosive-growth/780?utm_source=openai))

However, the prediction is about what happens **by March 2030**, not the situation in 2025. Given that multiple Chinese vendors have aggressive roadmaps and significant state backing, and several sources explicitly suggest parity *might* be achievable within about a decade, it is impossible at this stage to say confidently that China will *not* reach a competitive platform by the end of the five‑year window. ([c.poorc.com](https://c.poorc.com/t/chinas-domestic-gpu-industry-the-road-to-catching-up-amid-explosive-growth/780?utm_source=openai))

Therefore, the correct status of the prediction today is **“inconclusive” (too early to tell)**.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence by late 2025 shows that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has in fact become a broadly adopted standard interface for connecting LLMs to tools and services, in line with F’s prediction.

* **Adoption by major model providers:** Anthropic’s MCP is documented as being adopted by OpenAI and Google DeepMind shortly after its introduction, with integration into OpenAI products such as the ChatGPT desktop app, the Agents SDK, and the Responses API, and support in Google’s Gemini ecosystem. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_Context_Protocol?utm_source=openai))  Microsoft has also embraced MCP, adding native support in Windows and promoting it at Build 2025 as part of an “agentic web” vision, further cementing it as an industry standard. ([theverge.com](https://www.theverge.com/news/669298/microsoft-windows-ai-foundry-mcp-support?utm_source=openai))  MCP can also be integrated with Azure OpenAI and Microsoft’s Semantic Kernel, strengthening its position as the common interface layer around leading LLM platforms. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_Context_Protocol?utm_source=openai))

* **Ecosystem and usage scale:** The official MCP site describes it as a "universal adapter" and “USB‑C for AI” with growing adoption across major AI platforms including OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Microsoft. ([modelcontextprotocol.be](https://modelcontextprotocol.be/?utm_source=openai))  A 2025 empirical study finds MCP has effectively become the *de facto standard* for LLM tool integration, reporting over eight million weekly SDK downloads and nearly 1,900 open‑source MCP servers, which indicates large‑scale, real‑world uptake beyond a single vendor. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13538?utm_source=openai))  Another security-focused paper likewise characterizes MCP as having been “widely adopted” for connecting LLMs, tools, and data sources. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03767?utm_source=openai))

* **Cross‑industry tool/service integration:** Coverage aimed at practitioners (ITPro, Forbes, etc.) describes MCP as an open-source AI standard that is “gaining traction across the AI ecosystem” as a generic way for LLMs to interact with external databases, tools, and applications, explicitly positioning it as the solution to the N×M tool‑integration problem. ([itpro.com](https://www.itpro.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/what-is-model-context-protocol-mcp?utm_source=openai))  A TechRadar Pro piece notes that MCP-based workflows are already being pioneered by fintechs such as Stripe and Adyen, using MCP so that users can perform payment-related operations via natural language while the LLM handles the underlying API interactions—precisely the kind of “any LLM that uses MCP can interact with Stripe” scenario F described. ([techradar.com](https://www.techradar.com/pro/what-is-model-context-protocol-and-why-does-it-matter-to-software-engineers?utm_source=openai))

Across these independent sources, MCP is repeatedly described as an open standard, widely adopted or de facto standard for LLM–tool connections, with broad support from the top model providers and a growing third‑party ecosystem. That matches F’s prediction that MCP would become a standard, widely adopted interface for LLMs to integrate with external tools and services.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence from Nvidia’s financial results and industry reporting by late 2025 shows that the Blackwell generation has had an exceptionally strong commercial ramp, surpassing prior GPU generations.

By mid‑2025 (Q1 FY 2026), Nvidia reported that Blackwell already contributed nearly 70% of data‑center compute revenue and described it as the **fastest product ramp in the company’s history**, with major cloud providers rapidly deploying Blackwell GPUs at a pace of roughly 72,000 GPUs per week each. ([finance.yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/nvidia-leads-data-center-gpu-123100144.html?utm_source=openai))

By Q3 FY 2026 (quarter ended around October 2025), Nvidia’s data‑center revenue hit a record $51.2 billion—about 90% of total company sales—driven primarily by Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra. Management stated that Blackwell Ultra had become the **leading architecture across all customer categories**, while earlier Blackwell systems continued to see strong demand. Independent coverage of the same quarter notes overall record revenue of $57 billion, with **all GPUs effectively sold out** and the surge attributed to widespread adoption of Blackwell platforms. ([crn.com](https://www.crn.com/news/components-peripherals/2025/nvidia-blackwell-ultra-takes-lead-in-helping-drive-62-percent-growth-to-record-revenue?utm_source=openai))

Analyst commentary further underscores this: Nvidia’s CEO has been quoted saying **“Blackwell sales are off the charts, and cloud GPUs are sold out,”** with reports that Nvidia has secured more than **$500 billion in cumulative orders for Blackwell and its successor Rubin through the end of 2026**, indicating extraordinary demand visibility. ([investor.wedbush.com](https://investor.wedbush.com/wedbush/article/tokenring-2025-11-20-nvidias-ai-reign-intensifies-record-earnings-ignite-global-semiconductor-and-ai-markets?utm_source=openai))

Additional industry analysis notes that Nvidia remains on track to generate roughly **$500 billion in cumulative revenue from Blackwell and Rubin platforms by 2026**, with a substantial portion already delivered, reinforcing that this product cycle is unusually large in scale versus past generations. ([nationalcioreview.com](https://nationalcioreview.com/articles-insights/cio-field-notes/nvidia-continues-maximizing-on-ai-datacenter-growth-and-infrastructure-demand/?utm_source=openai))

Because Blackwell has (1) ramped faster than any prior Nvidia architecture on record, (2) driven unprecedented data‑center and total company revenues, and (3) remained supply‑constrained with very large, booked demand across major AI customers, F’s prediction that “Blackwell is going to be a very successful product cycle” relative to prior GPU generations has clearly come true by late 2025.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence shows that *Signalgate* did **not** fade from public and media attention within ~2–3 weeks of the leak; instead, it remained an active national‑security and political story for months.

Key points:

- The Signal leak was first widely publicized when Jeffrey Goldberg’s article in *The Atlantic* came out on 24–26 March 2025, with major outlets like *The Guardian* still describing the controversy as ongoing on 28 March ("continues through a fourth day"). Chamath’s prediction on 29 March therefore implied that by roughly mid‑April the matter would be largely forgotten. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2025/mar/27/signal-leak-us-politics-donald-trump-republicans-democrats-latest-news-updates?filterKeyEvents=false&page=with%3Ablock-67e57ef28f08287e917b189f&utm_source=openai))
- Well **beyond** that 2–3 week window, the Pentagon inspector general formally opened an investigation into Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s use of Signal, reported by multiple outlets on 3 April 2025, and InsideDefense published the IG’s notification letter the same day—coverage that treats Signalgate as a live, serious scandal, not something already forgotten. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/apr/03/pete-hegseth-signal-chat-dod-investigation?utm_source=openai))
- On 22 April 2025 (about three and a half weeks after the leak), watchdog group American Oversight filed a motion for a preliminary injunction in its *Signalgate* lawsuit, seeking emergency court orders to preserve Signal records—again generating fresh, national‑level coverage well past the predicted attention window. ([americanoversight.org](https://americanoversight.org/american-oversight-seeks-preliminary-injunction-in-signalgate-case-following-new-hegseth-revelations/?utm_source=openai))
- The story continued into the summer: a detailed Washington Post piece on 6 June 2025 covered the ongoing inspector‑general inquiry, and another on 23 July reported that Hegseth’s Signal messages drew on an email marked “SECRET/NOFORN,” directly contradicting administration denials. These are prominent, months‑later stories indicating sustained media interest. ([washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2025/06/06/hegseth-signalgate-inspector-general/?utm_source=openai))
- The episode has enduring visibility: it is documented in multiple up‑to‑date encyclopedia entries (English "United States government group chat leaks," German "Signalgate‑Affäre," Chinese and French pages), all treating *Signalgate* as a named, notable scandal of Trump’s second term—evidence that it was not quickly forgotten even in the longer run. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government_group_chat_leaks?utm_source=openai))

Because *Signalgate* remained under investigation, in court, and in major media coverage for months after late March 2025, the prediction that it would be largely forgotten within roughly two Scaramuccis (about 2–3 weeks) is best judged as **wrong**.

The Signalgate incident involved a Signal group chat leak of Yemen war plans (March 11-15, 2025), publicly revealed by The Atlantic on March 24, 2025 [Wikipedia; Atlantic via multiple sources]. Chamath's prediction on the March 29, 2025 All-In podcast was that attention would substantially die down and be largely forgotten within 2-3 weeks (~April 14-24) from the incident.

However, media coverage and fallout persisted well beyond:
- April: IG probe (Apr 3), Wired (Apr 15), NYT second chat (Apr 20), Foreign Affairs (Apr 24) [NYT, Wired, Foreign Affairs].
- May: Waltz resignation with Signalgate timelines (May 1), NBC photo (May 2) [USA Today, NBC].
- June-July: Hegseth impact (Jun 13), Waltz grilled at UN hearing (Jul 15) [BBC, Politico].
- Later: Jokes at Nov 7 event [The Hill].

No sharp decline by mid-April; ongoing investigations and consequences prove it was not 'largely forgotten' quickly [Politico Playbook Mar 25; 'staying power' podcasts Mar 27]. Current low mentions (Dec 2025) irrelevant to timeline.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction is framed with a multi‑year horizon: that, as pending cases over officials’ use of private/ephemeral communications progress and in light of the Signalgate incident, U.S. law and policy *will* develop significantly clearer rules and consequences over the next few years.

Since the podcast (late March 2025), there **have** been concrete moves toward clearer policy on messaging apps and recordkeeping:

- The National Archives issued AC 23.2025 on May 2, 2025, explicitly addressing records created on third‑party messaging apps like Signal and WhatsApp. It reiterates that messages about agency business are federal records regardless of platform, sets out obligations when personal accounts are used (copy or forward to an official account within 20 days), details penalties for unlawful destruction, and warns that auto‑delete features can violate record‑keeping rules unless records are preserved first. It also clarifies what counts as a transitory vs non‑transitory message and how retention schedules apply. ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/records-mgmt/memos/ac-23-2025?utm_source=openai))
- Reporting indicates that, shortly after Signalgate, the White House instructed staff at the U.S. DOGE Service that work‑related messages sent on personal devices and on Signal must be archived, that auto‑delete must be disabled, and that the baseline rule is to preserve all work‑related communications regardless of format. ([e-pluribusunum.org](https://e-pluribusunum.org/2025/03/28/chief-records-officer-of-the-united-states-says-blog-posts-and-signal-messages-are-public-records/?utm_source=openai))
- Individual agencies have updated or reiterated policies requiring preservation of email, text, and instant messages that meet the definition of a federal record, prohibiting use of personal messaging accounts for agency business unless records are promptly forwarded to official systems. Recent examples include HHS records‑management policy and GSA’s 2025 email/IT data retention directive. ([hhs.gov](https://www.hhs.gov/web/governance/digital-strategy/it-policy-archive/hhs-ocio-policy-for-records-management.html?utm_source=openai))
- In litigation stemming from Signalgate (American Oversight v. Hegseth), courts have ordered preservation of specific Signal chats and, in June 2025, ordered the acting archivist (Marco Rubio) to be notified about Signal chats at risk of deletion and to refer potential Federal Records Act violations to the attorney general for enforcement. That underscores the legal consequences side of the prediction. ([americanoversight.org](https://americanoversight.org/court-orders-rubio-to-refer-signalgate-record-violations-to-attorney-general-bondi/?utm_source=openai))

However, **several factors keep this from being judged "right" or "wrong" yet**:

- Much of the underlying legal framework (e.g., the content‑based definition of federal records and the extension of Capstone retention practices to electronic messages, including texts and third‑party apps) predates 2025. The 2025 developments largely clarify and reinforce existing rules rather than create a wholly new regime. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF12432?utm_source=openai))
- Ongoing controversies show that practice and enforcement are still unsettled. Watchdog groups continue to file complaints about officials using Signal with auto‑delete for official business even after Signalgate, arguing that this may violate the Federal Records Act and agency rules, which suggests that clarity and compliance are still being worked out. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/23/prosecutor-lindsey-halligan-auto-delete-chats?utm_source=openai))
- Most importantly, as of November 30, 2025 we are only about eight months into the "next few years" window the predictor invoked. There is still substantial time for additional legislation, regulations, and case law to emerge that could either strongly validate or undercut the claim that U.S. law and policy will become *significantly* clearer on which communications must be preserved versus can remain off the record.

Because the prediction is explicitly about developments *over the next few years* and we are still early in that period, with the legal/policy trajectory not yet fully settled, the status of the prediction is **too early to call**.

Only 8 months have passed by Dec. 1, 2025. Signalgate prompted lawsuits (e.g., American Oversight v. officials; judges ordered specific chat preservation in March 2025 but declined recovery of deleted messages in June), investigations (Pentagon IG on Hegseth), and NARA reminders (AC 23.2025, May 2025, reiterating existing Federal Records Act obligations and noting risks like Signal's disappearing messages). No new laws, amendments to the Federal Records Act, or comprehensive guidelines clarifying 'which categories must be preserved vs. off-record' have emerged. Heightened awareness and archiving tool interest exist, but no significant policy development yet. Too early to evaluate.
